summary:
Djibouti does not explicitly criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Articles 353 and 354 of the penal code refer vaguely to "good morals" and to obscene or public-morality offences without naming same-sex relations, and no statute states the position either way. Authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these provisions, and the country's at-a-glance legal assessment marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the territory. The practical result is that same-sex conduct is treated as de facto illegal even though no explicit offence exists on the books.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people, so a trans visitor who is visible or who engages in any same-sex conduct in public faces exposure to prosecution on that basis. There is no reported case law defining the limits of these articles, and no guarantee of how they are applied to a foreign national.

No legal gender recognition procedure exists. A trans visitor cannot obtain or amend an identity document reflecting their gender under Djibouti law, and there is no statutory route by which a passport or other document issued by another country would be recognised as consistent with a presented gender marker.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Djibouti. There is consequently no community infrastructure, no support or outreach services, and no organisation to contact in an emergency. The absence of any such body also means there is no domestic monitoring of how the public-morality provisions are enforced.

No legal prohibition of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in general law. The only protection reported is in the employment field, and it is not accompanied by any wider equality framework, hate-crime provision, or anti-violence mechanism.

Societal conditions are hostile. Sexual orientation and gender identity are treated as taboo, public societal discussion of homosexuality is not tolerated, and social and religious intolerance is pervasive. People fear family and community shunning if they are disclosed, which makes reporting to authorities unlikely and self-concealment the ordinary strategy.

The state does operate a complaint route: allegations can be filed with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH). No cases of official violence against LGBTI people are citable in the reporting period, which reflects the absence of documentation rather than a demonstrated record of protection.
tangentialFactors:
Djibouti's wider political environment shapes how any legal provision would be enforced. Reporting on the country documents suppression of the opposition and harsh prison conditions, alongside other serious rights concerns including female genital mutilation and trafficking. A state that treats political dissent this way offers no realistic expectation that a marginalised foreign national would obtain discretionary protection.

The evidence base for the country's treatment of sexual minorities has been thin for a long period. A Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board research response covering 2009 to March 2012 found documentation scarce across all consulted sources and relied on the 2010 United States country report as its principal reference, indicating how little legal, protective or support framework existed at that time. The 2015 United States State Department report contained only limited LGBT-specific content and served mainly as a historical baseline. The 2023 United States State Department report is the most recent detailed account available here.

Compared with jurisdictions that have explicit decriminalising statutes, a constitutional equality clause, or a functioning gender-recognition process, Djibouti offers none of these. The ambiguity of the penal code is itself a risk factor: conduct that is not named in law can still be prosecuted under a morality provision, and the visitor has no advance way to know where the line sits.
localsOnly:
Residents have a narrow employment discrimination protection, which is the only equality safeguard reported in Djiboutian law. No broader prohibition on discrimination grounds covers housing, education, health care, or public services.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable to residents as well as visitors. There is no administrative or judicial procedure for changing the gender marker on a national identity document or civil registry entry.

Residents who wish to organise collectively cannot register an LGBTI association, so no lawful domestic advocacy body exists. Complaints about mistreatment can be lodged with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH), though the reporting indicates no established practice of following such complaints through.

Disclosure carries substantial social cost. Orientation and gender identity are treated as taboo, no public discussion of homosexuality is tolerated, and the reported pattern is one of discrimination rather than of reported, prosecuted official violence. Fear of family and community shunning constrains how far residents can seek help.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sourced statements on discrimination protection do not align: one describes protection as existing in employment only, while the United States State Department's 2023 report states that there is no legal prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Whether an employment-level protection exists in practice, and whether it covers gender identity, is unresolved on this inventory.

No cases of official violence against LGBTI people are citable from the available reporting, and the inventory contains no documented instance of the public-morality provisions being applied to a trans person specifically. Whether articles 353 and 354 have been used against trans individuals, and with what outcome, is not sourced here.

The most recent detailed human-rights reporting in this inventory is from 2023. Whether the penal code articles have been amended, whether any registration decision on LGBTI organisations has changed, and whether any gender-recognition procedure has been introduced since then is unresolved.

Documentation of the treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti has been scarce across independent research sources for well over a decade, so the absence of adverse findings should not be read as evidence of safety.
